title: Acute Ischemic Stroke: Last Known Well Is a Treatment Vital Sign
bottomLine: Sudden focal neurologic deficit is a stroke emergency. Determine last-known-well time, activate the stroke pathway, check glucose, protect airway/oxygenation, keep the patient NPO until swallowing is screened, and prepare for rapid imaging and reperfusion evaluation. Do not 'watch and wait' for symptoms to resolve.
recognize: Sudden face/arm/leg weakness or numbness, especially one-sided
Speech/language change, visual loss, neglect, severe imbalance, or abrupt focal deficit
Posterior circulation stroke may present with severe vertigo/ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, weakness, or altered consciousness
Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke and must be checked rapidly
assess: Exact last known well and symptom discovery time
Focused neurologic assessment, glucose, BP, airway/breathing, SpO2, rhythm
Medication history including anticoagulants and recent surgery/bleeding
Repeat neuro checks for improvement or deterioration
actions: Activate stroke response/EMS immediately
Keep NPO until swallow safety is established
Obtain/prepare for emergent noncontrast brain imaging and other stroke studies
Administer thrombolytic or other ordered therapy only after eligibility is determined by the stroke team
Prepare for thrombectomy transfer/workflow when indicated
diagnostics: Noncontrast CT rapidly excludes intracranial hemorrhage but may be normal early in ischemic stroke
CTA/perfusion or MRI may guide thrombectomy/extended-window decisions
Do not delay brain imaging for nonessential tests
medicationSafety: Tenecteplase/alteplase can cause serious bleeding and require strict eligibility/BP monitoring
Antiplatelet/anticoagulant timing after stroke depends on hemorrhage exclusion and treatment plan
Avoid intensive glucose lowering that increases severe hypoglycemia risk
redFlags: Severe uncontrolled BP in a reperfusion candidate
teaching: Teach FAST/BE-FAST warning signs and EMS activation
Do not drive a possible stroke patient to a clinic when emergency stroke treatment is time dependent
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes stroke, establishes last-known-well, checks glucose, performs focused neuro monitoring, supports ordered therapy, and escalates. Thrombolysis/thrombectomy eligibility decisions are made by the authorized stroke team.
examTrap: Giving food, water, or oral medication before swallow screening because the patient can speak clearly.
oneLinePearl: Stroke: time, glucose, CT, NPO, neuro trend.
sourceBasis: 2026 AHA/ASA Guideline for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke

title: Intracerebral Hemorrhage: Neuro Decline, Blood Pressure, and Bleeding Expansion
bottomLine: Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage can expand rapidly. Sudden focal deficit, severe headache, vomiting, seizure, or declining consciousness requires emergency neuroimaging, close airway/neuro/BP monitoring, and rapid reversal of anticoagulation when ordered. New deterioration may mean hematoma expansion, hydrocephalus, herniation, or seizure.
recognize: Acute focal deficit with headache/vomiting or decreased consciousness
Very high BP may accompany ICH
Anticoagulant use increases concern for expansion
Posterior fossa hemorrhage can deteriorate quickly from brainstem compression/hydrocephalus
assess: Serial neuro exams/GCS or unit scale, pupils, BP, airway, oxygenation
Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet history and last dose
Monitor glucose, temperature, seizure activity and signs of rising ICP
actions: Activate stroke/neurosurgical emergency pathway
Maintain airway and head positioning per ordered neuro plan
Administer BP-lowering and anticoagulant-reversal therapy as ordered
Prepare for repeat imaging/neurosurgical intervention when deterioration occurs
diagnostics: Noncontrast CT identifies acute hemorrhage
Repeat imaging may assess expansion
Coagulation tests help guide some reversal strategies but do not replace medication history
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant reversal is drug-specific and time sensitive
Avoid routine prophylactic antiseizure medication unless indicated by the clinical plan; treat actual seizures promptly
BP therapy requires close monitoring to avoid hypotension
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce BP control and anticoagulant safety/follow-up
Teach family that sudden neurologic worsening after initial stabilization is an emergency
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs frequent focused neuro/hemodynamic monitoring where unit policy permits, administers ordered medications, and reports even subtle deterioration immediately. Reversal/surgical decisions are team-directed.
examTrap: Assuming improvement in headache means the hemorrhage is stable while level of consciousness is declining.
oneLinePearl: ICH danger is expansion—neuro trend and consciousness are critical.
sourceBasis: 2022 AHA/ASA Guideline for Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage

title: Increased ICP: Protect the Brain From Secondary Injury
bottomLine: The earliest dangerous clue in rising intracranial pressure is often a change in level of consciousness or neurologic exam. Maintain oxygenation and venous drainage, avoid unnecessary stimulation/straining, keep head/neck aligned as ordered, and escalate pupil, motor, or consciousness changes before late Cushing findings appear.
recognize: Early: restlessness, confusion, decreasing alertness, headache/vomiting, focal change
Progressive: pupillary change, abnormal posturing, worsening motor response
Late: hypertension with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations
assess: Serial LOC/GCS, pupils, motor strength/posturing, vital signs, SpO2
Assess pain/agitation, coughing, fever, urinary retention/constipation that can raise ICP demand/pressure
Monitor sodium/osmolality and ICP values if invasive monitoring is present
actions: Maintain head-of-bed/head-neck positioning per neuro order, often head elevated with neutral alignment
Prevent hypoxemia/hypotension and unnecessary Valsalva
Cluster care thoughtfully but do not postpone essential neuro checks
Administer ordered hyperosmolar therapy/antiseizure medication and monitor response
diagnostics: CT/MRI identify mass effect, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, edema
Lumbar puncture may be dangerous when mass lesion/marked ICP is suspected; do not assume it is routine
medicationSafety: Mannitol: monitor volume status, renal function and osmolality per protocol
Hypertonic saline: monitor sodium/osmolality and access/infusion requirements
Sedatives can obscure neuro assessment; monitor carefully
redFlags: Sudden loss of ICP waveform/drain issue with deterioration
teaching: Explain why coughing/straining/stimulation may be limited and why frequent neuro checks are necessary
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN neuro-critical-care participation varies by setting. The non-negotiable role is recognizing and immediately reporting neurologic trend changes; invasive ICP drain manipulation is restricted to trained authorized staff.
examTrap: Waiting for bradycardia and hypertension before reporting a patient who is becoming progressively harder to arouse.
oneLinePearl: LOC changes early; Cushing signs are late.

title: Seizure and Status Epilepticus: Safety, Time, Airway
bottomLine: During a seizure, protect from injury, maintain airway positioning/oxygenation, time the event, and do not place anything in the mouth or restrain the patient. A prolonged seizure or repeated seizures without recovery is status epilepticus and requires emergency benzodiazepine-first treatment per protocol and rapid escalation.
recognize: Generalized convulsive seizure may cause tonic-clonic movement, apnea/cyanosis, salivation, incontinence, postictal confusion
Focal seizures may present with localized movement, sensory symptoms, automatisms, or impaired awareness
Nonconvulsive status can present as persistent unexplained altered mental status
assess: Time onset/duration and observe movement, gaze, responsiveness, color/breathing
After seizure, assess airway, breathing, glucose, injury, neuro status and return to baseline
Review missed antiseizure meds, fever/infection, alcohol withdrawal, pregnancy, metabolic triggers
actions: Lower to safe surface, protect head, remove hazards, turn to side when feasible, loosen restrictive clothing
Suction/oxygen as needed after airway accessible
For status, activate emergency response and administer ordered benzodiazepine followed by longer-acting antiseizure therapy
diagnostics: Glucose is an immediate reversible cause check
Electrolytes, drug levels, imaging, toxicology, infection evaluation and EEG depend on context
EEG is important for suspected nonconvulsive status
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can depress respirations; prepare airway support
Phenytoin/fosphenytoin and other agents have infusion-specific cardiac/interaction risks
Abrupt withdrawal of antiseizure medications can precipitate seizures
redFlags: Seizure lasting about 5 minutes or recurrent without recovery
teaching: Medication adherence, seizure precautions, driving/work restrictions according to state law, sleep/substance trigger management
Family should time seizures and know when to call EMS
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN follows seizure/emergency protocols, administers authorized rescue medications, and reports prolonged/recurrent events. State rules affect rescue-med delegation in community settings.
examTrap: Putting a tongue blade/spoon in the mouth or restraining the patient's limbs during convulsions.
oneLinePearl: Protect, position, time—nothing in the mouth.
sourceBasis: American Epilepsy Society status epilepticus guidance

title: Meningitis: Infection Control and Antibiotics Cannot Wait
bottomLine: Fever with severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status, petechial/purpuric rash, or seizure can signal acute meningitis. Stabilize first, initiate appropriate transmission precautions for suspected meningococcal disease, obtain ordered cultures promptly, and give empiric antibiotics without avoidable delay when bacterial meningitis is suspected.
recognize: Classic triad is not always complete
Infants/older adults may present atypically
Petechial/purpuric rash with systemic illness raises concern for meningococcemia
Sepsis, raised ICP and seizures are major complications
assess: Airway/breathing, perfusion, neuro status, pupils, rash, seizure activity, hydration
Implement droplet precautions for suspected meningococcal meningitis per CDC/facility guidance
Assess contacts/exposure only within public-health plan
actions: Emergency escalation and sepsis support
Obtain ordered blood cultures/CSF pathway without delaying antibiotics in an unstable patient
Administer empiric antibiotics/dexamethasone as ordered
Use seizure/ICP precautions when indicated
diagnostics: Lumbar puncture evaluates CSF when safe
Brain imaging may precede LP in selected patients with concern for mass effect/ICP
Blood cultures can identify bacterial cause
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice is age/risk-specific
Close contacts of meningococcal disease may need public-health-directed chemoprophylaxis; do not prescribe or distribute independently
teaching: Complete treatment and follow public-health instructions for contacts/vaccination
Teach that close-contact prophylaxis is organism/exposure specific
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN initiates required precautions per policy, gives ordered antimicrobials, performs neuro/sepsis monitoring, and escalates. LP and public-health prophylaxis decisions are clinician/public-health directed.
examTrap: Delaying antibiotics until after lumbar puncture in a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected bacterial meningitis.
oneLinePearl: Suspected bacterial meningitis: stabilize, isolate appropriately, culture fast, antibiotics fast.

title: Autonomic Dysreflexia: Remove the Trigger While You Lower the Risk
bottomLine: In a patient with spinal cord injury typically at or above T6, sudden severe hypertension with pounding headache, flushing/sweating above the lesion, bradycardia or other autonomic symptoms can be autonomic dysreflexia. Sit upright, loosen restrictive items, check bladder first, then bowel/skin and other triggers, monitor BP frequently, and escalate/medicate per protocol if pressure remains severe.
recognize: Sudden BP rise above the patient's baseline
Headache, flushing/sweating above lesion, nasal congestion, anxiety, gooseflesh below lesion
Common triggers: bladder distention/kinked catheter, bowel impaction, pressure injury, tight clothing, painful stimulus
assess: Immediately recheck BP and symptoms
Inspect urinary drainage for kinks/obstruction and bladder distention
If bladder trigger excluded, assess bowel/skin/other noxious stimuli according to safe protocol
actions: Sit upright and lower legs if possible
Loosen tight clothing/devices
Correct obvious urinary obstruction without unnecessary delay
Administer rapid-acting antihypertensive as ordered if trigger removal does not promptly control severe BP
Continue monitoring after resolution for recurrence
diagnostics: This is primarily a clinical emergency; diagnostics target unresolved trigger/complications after immediate actions
medicationSafety: Antihypertensives can cause sudden hypotension once the trigger is relieved; monitor closely
Avoid triggering vigorous rectal manipulation without appropriate anesthetic/protocol during an active episode
redFlags: No catheter drainage with distended bladder
teaching: Patients/caregivers should carry an emergency plan, prevent bladder/bowel problems, protect skin, and know their usual BP
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN can identify the syndrome, position, assess common triggers, manage catheter issues within competency, administer ordered medication, and escalate. Bowel disimpaction procedures during active dysreflexia require specific protocol/competency.
examTrap: Laying the patient flat because they feel dizzy/headachy, which can further raise cerebral blood pressure.
oneLinePearl: AD: sit up, BP, bladder first.
sourceBasis: Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine autonomic dysreflexia guidance

title: Myasthenia Gravis: Is This Weakness a Breathing Problem?
bottomLine: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable skeletal-muscle weakness; bulbar or respiratory weakness can become myasthenic crisis. Watch swallowing, voice, cough, secretion handling and respiratory strength—not just limb weakness—and escalate early because oxygen saturation can stay normal until ventilation fails.
recognize: Ptosis/diplopia, facial/bulbar weakness, fatigable speech/chewing/swallowing
Crisis: weak cough, pooling secretions, dysphagia, dyspnea, declining vital capacity or respiratory strength
Infection, surgery, medication changes and missed therapy can trigger worsening
assess: Airway, respiratory effort, cough, secretion control, speech/swallow
Trend ordered respiratory mechanics such as vital capacity/NIF
Review medications that can worsen neuromuscular transmission
actions: Keep suction/airway support available and escalate respiratory decline
Schedule meals/rest when strength is best and follow swallow precautions
Administer pyridostigmine/immunotherapy as ordered and coordinate timing with meals when helpful
diagnostics: Antibody/electrodiagnostic testing supports diagnosis
Respiratory mechanics guide crisis severity better than waiting for desaturation
medicationSafety: Excess cholinesterase inhibitor can cause muscarinic effects and weakness; do not simply give extra doses for unexplained worsening
Magnesium and several antibiotic/antiarrhythmic classes can worsen MG in susceptible patients—verify new medications
teaching: Take medications on schedule, plan rest, report infection/worsening swallowing or breathing, and verify new drugs with the care team
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes bulbar/respiratory decline, maintains aspiration precautions, gives ordered therapy, and escalates. Ventilatory thresholds and plasma exchange/IVIG decisions are specialty-team directed.
examTrap: Waiting for low SpO2 before escalating a patient with weak cough, shallow breathing, and inability to clear secretions.
oneLinePearl: In MG, swallowing and cough tell you when weakness is becoming an airway crisis.

title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Ascending Weakness Can Reach Breathing
bottomLine: Guillain-Barré syndrome can progress from symmetric ascending weakness and areflexia to respiratory failure and autonomic instability. Trend respiratory strength, swallowing, heart rate/BP and weakness progression; escalating bulbar/respiratory symptoms require higher-acuity support before overt hypoxemia develops.
recognize: Symmetric tingling/weakness often beginning in legs and moving upward
Reduced/absent reflexes
Facial/bulbar weakness
Autonomic swings: tachy/bradycardia, hypertension/hypotension, urinary/ileus problems
assess: Serial motor strength and ability to lift head/cough/swallow
Ordered vital capacity/NIF or respiratory mechanics
Continuous or frequent HR/BP/rhythm in progressive disease
Pain and immobility complications
actions: Escalate rapidly progressive weakness or respiratory/bulbar involvement
Support airway and prepare for ventilation when indicated
Administer IVIG or plasma exchange as ordered
VTE, pressure-injury, aspiration, bowel/bladder and mobility prevention
diagnostics: CSF may show elevated protein with few cells after early disease
Nerve-conduction studies support diagnosis
Do not delay respiratory monitoring while waiting for confirmatory tests
medicationSafety: Corticosteroids are not effective routine treatment for classic GBS
IVIG has thrombosis/renal/infusion risks; plasma exchange has line/hemodynamic risks
teaching: Recovery often takes time; preserve mobility/skin and communicate expected rehabilitation without promising a fixed timeline
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors progression and complications, supports ordered therapy, and escalates early. Airway/IVIG/plasma-exchange management occurs in appropriately staffed settings.
examTrap: Assuming normal oxygen saturation means respiratory failure is not developing despite rapidly weakening respiratory muscles.
oneLinePearl: GBS climbs—watch the diaphragm and autonomic system before they fail.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Neurology/neuromuscular GBS guidance

title: Parkinson Disease: Mobility, Swallowing, and Medication Timing
bottomLine: Parkinson care is built around function and medication timing. Bradykinesia/rigidity/postural instability raise fall and aspiration risk, while missed or delayed dopaminergic doses can sharply worsen mobility. Give scheduled therapy on time, assess swallowing and orthostasis, and support safe movement without rushing the patient.
recognize: Bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor, shuffling/festination, freezing, reduced facial expression/voice
Nonmotor: constipation, depression, sleep problems, orthostatic hypotension, cognitive change
Dysphagia/sialorrhea increase aspiration risk
assess: Mobility/falls, swallowing/cough, nutrition/weight, orthostatic symptoms, bowel function, cognition/hallucinations
Correlate function with medication 'on/off' periods
Assess sudden confusion for delirium rather than automatically attributing it to Parkinson disease
actions: Administer levodopa/carbidopa at scheduled times
Use fall and aspiration precautions, therapy/mobility aids, constipation plan
Allow extra time for movement and cueing during freezing
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical; sudden acute decline should prompt evaluation for infection, medication issues, dehydration, injury or other acute cause
medicationSafety: Levodopa can cause orthostasis, nausea, dyskinesia/hallucinations
Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy can cause severe rigidity/hyperthermic syndrome
Dopamine-blocking antiemetics/antipsychotics can worsen parkinsonism; verify choices
redFlags: Severe acute rigidity/hyperthermia after missed therapy
Inability to take essential oral medication
teaching: Medication timing matters; do not skip doses because the patient is slow to swallow without obtaining an alternative plan
Use mobility and swallow strategies taught by therapy
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN gives scheduled medications, monitors function/swallow/falls, reinforces therapy strategies, and reports acute change. Medication formulation/regimen changes require prescriber/pharmacy direction.
examTrap: Giving Parkinson medication whenever convenient during the med pass rather than close to the patient's scheduled regimen.
oneLinePearl: Parkinson meds are time-critical because function follows the dose.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Neurology Parkinson disease practice guidance

title: Multiple Sclerosis: Relapse, Fatigue, Heat, and Function
bottomLine: MS symptoms can fluctuate with true inflammatory relapse or temporarily worsen with fever/heat/infection without new inflammation. Assess new neurologic change for infection, temperature, medication/adherence and functional impact; conserve energy, prevent falls/skin/bladder complications, and report sustained new deficits for relapse evaluation.
recognize: Vision change/optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, weakness/spasticity, imbalance, fatigue, bladder dysfunction
Heat or fever can transiently worsen existing symptoms
New symptoms lasting beyond a transient trigger need clinical evaluation
assess: New versus baseline neuro deficit, infection/fever, mobility/falls, bladder retention/UTI, bowel function, fatigue, mood
Monitor disease-modifying therapy infection/lab risks as ordered
Assess skin and equipment needs when mobility reduced
actions: Treat infection/fever according to the plan
Use cooling/energy conservation and assistive devices
Administer ordered corticosteroid for significant relapse and disease-modifying therapy on schedule
Prevent urinary/pressure/mobility complications
diagnostics: MRI and neurologic evaluation help assess disease activity
A urine test may be appropriate when urinary infection could explain pseudo-relapse
medicationSafety: Disease-modifying therapies have agent-specific infection, liver, blood-cell, pregnancy or infusion risks
Steroids shorten recovery from selected relapses but do not replace long-term disease-modifying therapy
teaching: Energy conservation, cooling, fall prevention, vaccination/infection precautions according to therapy, and adherence to disease-modifying treatment
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN supports symptom management, medication monitoring, mobility/skin/bladder care, and reports sustained new deficits. Relapse diagnosis and disease-modifying therapy selection are specialty decisions.
examTrap: Assuming every temporary heat-related symptom flare means the disease has permanently progressed.
oneLinePearl: MS symptoms can flare from heat/infection without a new lesion—assess the trigger and duration.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Neurology multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapy guidance

title: Delirium vs Dementia: Acute Change Is a Medical Problem Until Proven Otherwise
bottomLine: Delirium is an acute/fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition and often signals illness, medication effect, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, withdrawal, pain, retention/constipation, or environmental stress. New confusion in a person with dementia is still new confusion—look for a reversible cause rather than writing it off as baseline.
recognize: Delirium: hours-to-days onset, fluctuating course, impaired attention, altered awareness
Dementia: usually chronic progressive cognitive decline with more stable alertness early
Hypoactive delirium is quiet and easily missed
assess: Compare with baseline using family/caregiver and prior chart
Check oxygenation, glucose, vitals, pain, medications, hydration, urinary/bowel issues, infection signs, sensory aids
Use a validated delirium screen when available
actions: Treat the underlying cause and maintain safety
Reorient gently, provide glasses/hearing aids, sleep-wake cues, hydration/nutrition, mobility
Avoid unnecessary restraints/catheters and high-risk sedating/anticholinergic medications
diagnostics: Testing is targeted to the clinical cause; routine broad panels without assessment are lower value
Urinalysis alone does not prove that bacteriuria caused delirium; correlate with symptoms and clinician evaluation
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can worsen most delirium except selected indications such as alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal
Anticholinergics, opioids, sedatives and polypharmacy are common contributors
teaching: Explain that delirium can fluctuate and recovery may lag after the trigger is treated; familiar voices/items and sensory aids can help
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN is well positioned to identify baseline-to-current change and precipitating bedside factors; report acute confusion promptly rather than treating it as expected aging.
examTrap: Assuming a confused older adult has a UTI solely because the urinalysis shows bacteria without assessing other causes or urinary symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Dementia is baseline; delirium is a change—change needs a cause.

title: Cauda Equina Syndrome: Back Pain With Bladder, Saddle, or Motor Red Flags
bottomLine: Severe low-back/radicular pain becomes a spinal emergency when accompanied by new urinary retention/overflow, saddle sensory loss, bilateral or progressive leg weakness, bowel dysfunction, or reduced anal tone. Keep the patient safe, perform focused neuro/bladder assessment, and escalate urgently for MRI and surgical evaluation.
recognize: Saddle/perineal numbness
New urinary retention or loss of bladder sensation
Bilateral sciatica or progressive motor weakness
Bowel dysfunction/sexual dysfunction in the right context
assess: Lower-extremity strength/sensation, gait when safe, perineal/saddle symptoms by appropriate clinician
Bladder symptoms and post-void residual when ordered
Pain onset, cancer/infection/trauma/anticoagulation risk
actions: Urgent spine/neurosurgical escalation
Keep fall precautions and manage bladder safely according to order
Prepare for emergent MRI/decompression when indicated
diagnostics: MRI is the key imaging test
Do not reassure based on pain intensity alone; neurologic/bladder signs determine urgency
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not delay evaluation or be used to explain away progressive neurologic findings
Anticoagulation history matters if spinal hematoma is possible
teaching: Patients with back pain should seek emergency care for new bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle numbness, or progressive weakness
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes the red-flag cluster, obtains focused data within role, protects mobility, and escalates urgently. Do not wait for routine outpatient follow-up.
examTrap: Treating new urinary retention in severe back pain as an opioid side effect without first excluding cauda equina/spinal compression.
oneLinePearl: Back pain + bladder/saddle weakness signs = spinal emergency.
